plan.concept: How the RANSAC algorithm iteratively proposes model hypotheses from minimal random samples and evaluates them using a consensus set of inliers.
learningObjectives: After engaging with this figure, the student will understand how RANSAC fits a model using a minimal sample set (two points for a line).
The student will be able to explain how the distance threshold distinguishes inliers from outliers.
The student will understand why the model with the highest consensus (most inliers) is selected as the winning fit.
plan.keyInsight: By generating candidate models from just two random points at a time, RANSAC can discover the true underlying trend even when the dataset is dominated by extreme outliers.

interactions.label: RANSAC Iteration
interactions.effect: Changes the two randomly selected points (highlighted in red), the fitted line, and updates which points are classified as inliers (blue) or outliers (hollow black).
interactions.teaches: Demonstrates how different random pairs of points yield wildly different candidate models, some of which align with the true data distribution and others that do not.

interactions.label: Inlier Threshold
interactions.effect: Visually widens or narrows a shaded 'tolerance band' corridor around the candidate line, dynamically updating which points fall inside (turning blue) or outside.
interactions.teaches: Shows how the threshold parameter directly controls the sensitivity of the consensus step—too narrow misses valid data; too wide includes noise and outliers.

demo_steps.title: Analyze a poor hypothesis
demo_steps.narration: Look at this initial iteration where RANSAC randomly picked two points (red circles) that happen to lie on a horizontal line. Notice how only two other points (blue circles) fall close enough to this line to be counted as inliers, giving us a low total consensus of 4 inliers.
demo_steps.focus: The horizontal red line, the two red sample points, the two blue inliers, and the text label reading '4 inliers'.

demo_steps.title: Try another random sample
demo_steps.narration: Let's step to the next iteration. Now, RANSAC has picked a completely different pair of points. Notice how this new candidate line fits the dataset even worse, leaving almost all other points categorized as outliers (hollow black circles). This hypothesis will quickly be discarded due to its low consensus score.
demo_steps.focus: The newly angled line and the high concentration of hollow outlier circles far away from it.

demo_steps.title: Discover the true consensus
demo_steps.narration: Now look what happens when the random sample happens to pick two points aligned with the true diagonal trend of the data. Suddenly, a large majority of the points fall within our threshold band. This high consensus (e.g., 8 inliers) tells RANSAC that it has found a highly promising model.
demo_steps.focus: The diagonal red line passing cleanly through the main cluster of points, turning them blue.

demo_steps.title: Adjusting the tolerance
demo_steps.narration: Finally, try increasing the inlier threshold. Watch how the shaded tolerance corridor around the line expands. While a wider threshold can capture more true data points, setting it too high risks incorrectly labeling unrelated outliers as inliers, corrupting our final fit.
demo_steps.focus: The widening shaded region around the diagonal line and the addition of distant points changing color to blue.

plan.reconstructionNotes: An interactive scatter plot with an X and Y axis. Features 10-12 data points representing a noisy linear trend with several prominent outliers. Two specific points chosen for the current iteration are highlighted in solid red. A red candidate line passes exactly through these two red points. Points within the tolerance threshold of this line are colored solid light blue. A shaded tolerance band (corridor) is visible around the red line, with its thickness controlled by the threshold slider. Points outside this corridor are drawn as hollow circles with black outlines. A text label dynamically updates to display the count of inliers (e.g., 'X inliers').
